title: Advanced Dataclasses, Validation and Immutable Records
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of Advanced Dataclasses, Validation and Immutable Records.

understand.concept: The dataclasses module generates common methods such as __init__ and __repr__ from annotated fields. Advanced options support immutable-style records, ordering, slots, keyword-only fields and post-initialization checks. field(default_factory=...) creates a fresh mutable default per instance. Dataclasses reduce boilerplate but do not automatically validate arbitrary field values.
understand.whyItMatters: Dataclasses make data-oriented application models concise and predictable while keeping domain logic close to the data.
understand.analogy: A dataclass is a preprinted form with standard fields and routine handling already prepared.
understand.analogyLimit: A generated form does not verify every business rule unless the application adds explicit validation.
understand.summary: Advanced Dataclasses, Validation and Immutable Records develops practical application engineering skills for Python projects.

explain.narrative:
## Model application data
Use `@dataclass` for records whose fields define their main purpose. Use `default_factory` for mutable defaults, `frozen=True` when reassignment should be prevented, `slots=True` when a fixed attribute layout is appropriate, and `__post_init__` for invariant checks. Frozen dataclasses are shallowly immutable: mutable objects stored in fields can still change. Use `dataclasses.replace` to create a modified copy.

examples.title: Generate a data record
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class Product:
    name: str
    price: float
item = Product('Notebook', 25.0)
print(item)
examples.explanation: The decorator generates a readable representation and initializer.

examples.title: Use a fresh list per instance
examples.explanation: default_factory prevents instances from sharing one mutable list.

examples.title: Validate after initialization
examples.explanation: __post_init__ runs after generated initialization and can enforce domain rules.

examples.title: Create a modified copy
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int
p = Point(2, 3)
q = replace(p, x=8)
print(p.x, q.x)
examples.explanation: replace creates a new instance with selected fields changed.

examples.title: Use slots for declared fields
examples.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass(slots=True)
class Coordinate:
    x: int
    y: int
point = Coordinate(4, 5)
print(point.x + point.y, hasattr(point, '__dict__'))
examples.explanation: slots=True avoids the usual per-instance __dict__ for declared attributes.

practise.guidedTask: Create a dataclass for an order line with quantity and unit price. Use __post_init__ to reject negative values and default_factory for mutable collections.
practise.independentTask: Model a configuration record with a frozen dataclass. Explain whether nested mutable values would still be protected.
hints: Use field(default_factory=list) for per-instance mutable values.
frozen=True prevents normal field reassignment, not deep mutation.
replace returns a new dataclass instance.
slots=True changes attribute storage; measure before using it for optimization.
practise.challenge: Design dataclasses for an invoice and its line items, validate invariants and compute totals without storing stale derived values.
